item.title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. We studied 101 youths aged 8-18 years using brain entropy (BEN), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Voxelwise and seven-network models evaluated age associations and task-by-age interactions while adjusting for sex, head motion, and gray-matter anatomy. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF-AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain-behavior coupling.

item.title: Neural correlates of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance, EEG, and MRI dataset
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed). High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset. Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.

item.title: Reconsidering the Psychotomimetic Properties of LSD: Connectome-Based Classification Reveals Partial Overlap with First Episode Psychosis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The acute effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) have long been compared to early psychosis. Despite this, no studies have compared the acute effects of LSD and psychosis on resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) with parallel approaches. We used connectome-based classification, a data-driven method, to distinguish between medication-naïve, non-affective first episode psychosis (FEP) and the acute effects of LSD. Separate classifiers were trained to distinguish the acute effects of LSD from placebo and FEP patients from matched healthy controls. The LSD-placebo classifier was then validated on an external LSD-placebo dataset. The network-interaction classifiers with good discriminability were then applied across datasets to evaluate whether LSD-related connectivity patterns could classify FEP as being LSD-like and vice versa. Subsequently, we investigated univariate RSFC between select networks, based on which network-interactions the classifiers suggested might overlap in LSD and FEP. Cross-application of externally validated LSD-placebo classifiers revealed partial overlap between LSD and FEP, particularly involving the dorsal attention network (DAN) and sensorimotor network (SMN). Application of the most discriminant FEP-HC network-interaction classifiers revealed that LSD displayed select similarities with FEP. Univariate network analysis also supports between-network DAN and SMN dysconnectivity being a point of convergence. Our findings indicate that neural correlates of FEP might have select overlaps with changes in brain functioning produced by LSD. These results suggest serotonergic dysfunction might play a role in the early stages of psychosis and necessitate future studies directly comparing FEP and LSD.

item.title: Spatial trapping and anteroposterior segregation of the default mode network in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The spatial organisation of the default mode network (DMN) across recurrent brain configurations remains poorly understood in schizophrenia. Here, we introduce two indices to quantify how selectively a network is represented across brain modes and whether selected anterior and posterior regions participate in the same configurations. Resting-state functional MRI from 16 healthy controls and 11 participants with non-acute schizophrenia was used to assess static and dynamic functional connectivity, global synchronisation, intrinsic ignition and variability measures. Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis identified the brain modes. The Spatial Trapping Index (STI) measured the distribution of relative network composition across four modes, while anterior–posterior co-participation (CAP) measured shared these modes. The two indices were compared using permutation test within Holm correction. Static functional connectivity was lower within the dorsal attention network, while dynamic functional connectivity showed greater variability in several network. No significant differences were detected in global synchronisation, intrinsic ignition or the three signatures of metastability. Mean DMN composition was similar between groups, but STI was higher in SCZ, while CAP was lower. Bootstrap resampling retained the observed directions in 89.6% of STI contrasts and 91.9% of CAP contrasts. These findings suggest that DMN representation is less selective across brain modes in schizophrenia, while selected anterior and posterior regions participate less consistently together. STI and CAP offer a new way to quantify these complementary aspects of spatial organisation, providing a basis for investigating their clinical relevance.

item.title: Saccadic network dysfunction underlies eye-movement variability in early Parkinson's disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by altered subcortical-cortical connectivity, leading to motor and cognitive deficits. Saccadic eye movement abnormalities are among the earliest and most persistent markers of the disease, serving as sensitive indicators of disrupted oculomotor and cognitive control. While changes in average saccadic behavioral measures are widely reported in Parkinson's disease, intra-individual variability in saccadic performance and the underlying network dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we quantified intra-individual saccadic variability in early-stage Parkinson’s disease and identified its functional correlates within the resting-state saccadic network. We analyzed data from the inclusion visit of 91 patients with early-stage Parkinson’s disease and 46 healthy controls from the ICEBERG cohort (monocentric prospective research study) who underwent oculomotor testing and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. First, at the behavioral level, we assessed intra-individual variability in saccadic performance within each group using the coefficient of variation of reaction time and normalized peak velocity across trials. Second, at the brain level, we assessed group differences in static and dynamic functional connectivity across 39 regions comprising the saccadic network. We examined the relationship between network connectivity and saccadic variability using partial least squares analysis. We also quantified network organization using graph-theory measures of global efficiency and clustering coefficient. Finally, we tested the relevance of intra-individual saccadic variability and network features in distinguishing patients from healthy controls using a multivariate Mahalanobis classifier. Our results showed that, compared to HC, patients had higher intra-individual variability in saccadic behavioral measures of reaction time (p Holm = 0.012) and normalized peak velocity (p Holm = 0.012). Interestingly, patients had (i) reduced static and dynamic connectivity within the saccadic network and (ii) weaker associations between network connectivity and intra-individual saccadic variability of specifically normalized peak velocity. These results were particularly driven by regions within the cognitive saccade network. The classifier that integrated intra-individual saccadic variability and network connectivity achieved 95.62% accuracy in distinguishing patients from healthy controls, with dynamic connectivity contributing more strongly to classification performance than static connectivity. We demonstrate that elevated intra-individual variability of saccades, underpinned by altered functional connectivity within cognitive-oculomotor networks, is a prominent feature of early-stage Parkinson’s disease. Emerging as a promising physiological marker of disease pathophysiology, intra-individual variability offers a powerful new framework to refine early diagnosis and improve the tracking of neurodegeneration before severe clinical milestones are reached.

item.title: Early Neural Responses to Negative Emotional Processing and Longitudinal Grief Trajectories in Later Life.
item.description:
Psychotherapy and psychosomatics
Introduction While most bereaved adults adapt to their loss within a year, 3-10% develop Prolonged Grief Disorder. The neurobiological substrates of adaptive versus maladaptive grief trajectories remain poorly understood. Methods In this longitudinal study, ninety-seven adults (50-83 years) bereaved within the past year completed task-based fMRI (an emotional face-matching paradigm) and resting-state fMRI at study baseline. Grief symptoms were repeatedly assessed over 12 months. Voxel-wise linear mixed-effects models with cluster-wise correction (uncorrected p=.005; alpha=.05) examined associations between baseline fMRI responses to negative emotional faces (fearful and angry) versus shapes and 12-month symptom trajectories, adjusting for demographics, time since loss, and depressive symptoms. Results At baseline, left anterior insula activity was positively associated with loneliness (r=.305) and intrusive thoughts (r=.328). Longitudinally, greater baseline activity in bilateral anterior insula and left amygdala was associated with faster improvement in loneliness (z<-3.01). Lower amygdala-orbitofrontal cortex resting-state connectivity was associated with faster loneliness improvement, with stronger effects at higher depressive symptoms and greater perceived social support. Conversely, greater left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity (z=3.10) and its task-dependent connectivity with lateral occipital cortices (z=3.18) were associated with slower improvement in avoidant coping. Conclusion Greater engagement of salience network circuit components during negative emotional processing was associated with diminishing loneliness, whereas greater recruitment of prefrontal executive control network node was associated with persistent avoidance. These findings suggest distinct neural pathways underlying adaptive versus maladaptive grief responses. Further research to confirm these observations and to develop early risk stratification and mechanism-informed interventions to prevent prolonged grief is needed.

item.title: Remodeling stress-responsive networks following early life adversity: Insights from preclinical models.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup. Preclinical models using primates and rodents have allowed for fine control over these variables, providing substantial evidence of pathways and related biomarkers impacted by ELA. The present review aims to bridge findings from human clinical data with preclinical research, highlighting well-supported ELA-induced changes in the functional connectivity of stress-sensitive pathways, as well as alterations in additional cortical and subcortical pathways which are susceptible to disturbances during development. We also present key neuromodulatory mechanisms contributing to connectivity changes observed in preclinical models, and sex-specific nuances. Addressing these critical gaps could enhance the potential of connectivity-based therapeutic approaches. Lastly, we consider the translatability of functional connectivity analyses using various preclinical techniques for studying the influence of ELA on the developing brain.

item.title: Genetic, neural and early-environmental architecture of resilience
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Resilience is shaped by factors ranging from the genome through early-life experience to the brain, yet its biological basis in humans remains unclear because studies have rarely integrated these levels and have been confined to small samples. Using the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) and multimodal data from tens of thousands of UK Biobank (UKB) participants, with replication in Generation Scotland (GS), we found that resting-state functional connectivity, particularly within the flexibility and valuation networks, is a robust neural correlate of resilience. Resilience also showed a generalizable genetic basis: a polygenic score (PGS) derived from a UKB genome-wide association study predicted BRS in GS. Genes and childhood experiences converged on the flexibility network through distinct routes: the polygenic association with resilience was partly explained by central executive-salience integration, whereas childhood experiences were associated with default-mode-centered integration. By separating genetically anchored from experience-sensitive routes, these findings point to network targets that interventions could tailor to the sources of an individual's vulnerability.

item.title: Reduced Resting Brain Entropy and Structural-Functional Reorganization in Hearing Loss
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. We examined this question using multimodal MRI from 52 adults with age-related hearing loss and 30 normal-hearing controls. Guided by convergent neuroimaging evidence, we focused on the superior temporal gyrus (STG) and assessed brain entropy (BEN), complementary resting-state measures, and gray matter volume (GMV). Hearing loss was associated with lower BEN in a focal right-STG cluster after adjustment for local GMV (14 voxels; cluster FWER p = 0.008), consistent with more recurrent BOLD signal patterns. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. A separate whole-brain analysis revealed higher bilateral midcingulate cortex (MCC) GMV (FWE p = 0.002 and 0.015), motivating examination of the auditory-cingulate relationship. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Exploratory analyses suggested weaker directed STG-to-MCC influence alongside a small tractography-derived group difference. Exploratory directional comparisons indicated stronger right-MCC GMV-BEN coupling (p = 0.034) and STG-MCC SC-FC coupling (p = 0.037) in controls than in hearing loss. Together, these findings link greater temporal regularity in auditory association cortex to altered auditory-cingulate coordination and local structure-function correspondence, suggesting that adaptation to hearing loss involves both the organization of spontaneous cortical dynamics and their relationship to brain structure.

item.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

item.title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

item.title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

item.title: Social Connection: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Associations with Social Networks, and the Roles of Empathy and Sex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Smaller social networks (SNs) negatively influence cognition, psychiatric trajectories and mortality. Studies linking SNs to resting-state functional connectivity (FC) inconsistently suggest orbito-frontal and frontoparietal regions and implicate a potential role for empathy and sex. We investigate how SN characteristics relate to FC, additionally assessing if empathy and sex alter these associations. Group-independent component analysis was applied to multi-band resting-state fMRI from 83 participants (Caltech Conte dataset: ds003798). The Social Network Index measures SN-contacts (SN-contacts) SN-diversity (number of roles) and SN-embeddedness (number of contact groups) and the Empathy Quotient measured empathy. Using MANCOVA, we investigate if resting-state network power and connectivity are associated with SNI measures and whether these relationships differ by empathizing ability and sex. Participants aged 18-48 (mean age 29.3+/-7.0, 55% male) demonstrated SN-contacts and SN-diversity associated with lower frontal-pole FC within the default-mode network (DMN, q-values<0.05). Empathy altered how SN-diversity and SN-contacts relate to superior lateral-occipital, default mode and salience network FC (q-values<0.05). Finally, males and females showed diverging associations of SN-contacts and SN-diversity with salience network power. Smaller SNs were associated with increased anterior-DMN FC, potentially indicating a tendency towards internally-directed cognition in more socially isolated individuals. Opposing relationships between SNs with salience and lateral-frontoparietal networks by empathy level highlights empathy as critical for understanding social biology. Males and females differed in SN associations with salience network coherency, supporting known sex-specific neural correlates of social behavior. These findings provide insights into the biology of social networks, offering potential targets for studying social deficits in psychiatric populations.

item.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

item.title: Advances in Neuroscience in an Age of Rapid Technological and AI Innovation – Towards Integration Across Scales
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation. Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next. Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a future-oriented framework for their integration. First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity. Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders. Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains. We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.

item.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

item.title: Connectome fingerprinting predicts prefrontal cortical activation during abstract reasoning.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Connectome fingerprinting (CF) is a machine-learning technique that uses an individual's unique brain connectivity profile to make predictions about their individual brain activity patterns. Previous studies have successfully employed CF using sensory, working memory, and auditory/visual functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data. Here, we demonstrate that this technique can be used to examine higher-order cognition and evaluate the effectiveness of the CF method in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), an area where brain function and structure has been shown to be exceptionally variable across individuals. We designed a CF model, using a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme, to predict individually-specific blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activation in the lateral PFC. We used an abstract reasoning task designed to probe higher-order cognitive function specific to the lateral PFC. Our results demonstrated that CF better predicts abstract reasoning activation in the lateral PFC compared to the group average. We also tested whether task-evoked BOLD activity could be predicted using a model trained on a subset of the functional connectome. We demonstrate that CF models trained on a partial connectome from associative brain networks achieved similar levels of model performance compared to models trained on the full connectome. We observed that model performance varied across participants, suggesting that within-participant reliability in task activation, and deviation from the group average influence the model. Overall, we used CF to characterize individuals' task-evoked BOLD activation during abstract reasoning, demonstrating a link between resting-state functional architecture and brain activations and identifying key networks that contribute to higher-order cognition.

item.title: Functional connectivity profile of the amygdala subfields associates with emotional well-being in aging.
item.description:
GeroScience
Amygdala-related functional connectivity (FC) plays a crucial role in human emotion, cognition, and mental well-being. The amygdala is a highly heterogeneous structure, with subregions that have both distinct and overlapping functions. However, the connectivity patterns of different amygdala subregions, and how these associations vary with age, remain poorly understood. Functional MRI data were analyzed from 68 younger adults and 66 older adults during movie watching in a 7-T MRI scanner. Partial least squares (PLS) analysis was used to identify latent variables capturing variance associated with age-related differences in the FC patterns of three amygdala subregions: the basolateral (BLA), centromedial (CMA), and superficial (SFA) nuclei. In addition, covariance between behavioral measures, including emotional resilience and cognitive function, and FC of these subregions were examined. We further explored correspondence with large-scale brain networks, the associated cognitive processes in Neurosynth, and the spatial distributions of neurotransmitter receptors of the identified connectivity patterns of the BLA, CMA, and SFA. Multivariate analyses revealed that functional connectivity patterns of amygdala subregions related to emotional resilience largely overlapped across widespread brain regions; however, their associations differed by age. During negative movie viewing, stronger coupling of amygdala subregions with the cortex were associated with higher emotional resilience in older adults but lower emotional resilience in younger adults. Associations with cognitive function were weaker and less consistent across subregions. The identified connectivity patterns were linked to the salience, control, and default mode networks and showed spatial correspondence with mGluR5 and 5-HT6 receptor distributions. These findings highlight age-dependent reorganization of amygdala-related networks that support emotional resilience and provide novel insights into the functional connectivity patterns associated with emotional well-being in younger and older adults.

item.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depressive Symptoms: A within-network resting-state functional connectivity study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the role of depressive symptoms in the relationship between CUD, cannabis use characteristics, and within-network resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) in the Executive Control (ECN), the Salience (SN), the Default Mode (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia (BGN) networks. Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD participants and 102 controls, we examined the associations of group, depressive symptoms, and their interaction with within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we assessed the associations between cannabis use characteristics, depressive symptoms, and RSFC. We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensitivity analysis in the largest contributing study (n = 187). Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the left ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a positive association between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals. The largest study analysis additionally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relative to controls. Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were positively associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negatively among those with lighter use. Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alterations within distinct networks. Group differences potentially emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity. This highlights the importance of accounting for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD participants and 102 controls, we examined the associations of group, depressive symptoms, and their interaction with within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we assessed the associations between cannabis use characteristics, depressive symptoms, and RSFC. We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensitivity analysis in the largest contributing study (n = 187). Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the left ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a positive association between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals. The largest study analysis additionally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relative to controls. Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were positively associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negatively among those with lighter use. Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alterations within distinct networks. Group differences potentially emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity. This highlights the importance of accounting for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

item.title: Age-related changes in brain connectivity: Cross-sectional and longitudinal effects.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Age-related changes in functional connectivity within and between brain networks may contribute to cognitive and behavioral decline in aging. Prior research has consistently reported declines in within-network connectivity with age, though findings on between-network connectivity change have been mixed. Most studies have relied on cross-sectional designs, making it difficult to disentangle age-related effects from confounding cohort effects. Therefore, this study utilizes both cross-sectional (between-subject) and longitudinal (within-subject) datasets and employs mixed-effects models to elucidate age-related changes in resting-state functional connectivity across eight large-scale brain networks. After clinical screening and motion-based quality control, analyses were based on resting-state fMRI from 53 younger adults and 127 older adults, 45 of whom were rescanned approximately 4 years later. We examined whole-brain within-network connectivity, between-network connectivity, and network segregation. Cross-sectionally, older age was associated with lower within-network (p < 0.001) and between-network connectivity (p = 0.003), whereas segregation showed a more modest cross-sectional reduction that was concentrated in the salience and visual networks. Longitudinally, over approximately 4 years both within-network (p = 0.003) and between-network (p = 0.003) connectivity declined, while segregation did not change (p = 0.546). Declines in within- and between-network connectivity were broad rather than network specific, with the Default Mode and Salience networks most consistently affected.

item.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
Introduction Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. Methods We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Results Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Conclusions Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

item.title: Inter-subject functional variability of gray and white matter during methadone maintenance treatment and its association with gene expression profiles.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Background Methadone maintenance treatment(MMT) for opioid use disorder(OUD) may cause changes in brain functional heterogeneity whose molecular mechanisms remain unknown. This study aims to investigate MMT-related gray/white matter inter-subject variability functional connectivity(GM/WM-IVFC) alterations and to associate them with clinical and transcriptomic characteristics. Methods Between March 2017 and June 2026, a total of 244 participants were voluntarily enrolled from detoxification centers, drug rehabilitation clinics, and society in Hunan Province, China, including MMT group(N = 44), individuals with sustained heroin self-abstinence and no lifetime MMT(HSA, N = 42), short-term abstinent heroin users at baseline(OUD1, N = 62) and 10-month opioid-free follow-up(OUD2, N = 43), and two healthy control cohorts(HC1, N = 48; HC2, N = 48) respectively age/gender-matched with MMT/HSA groups and OUD1. OUD1/2 and HSA groups were used to exploratively investigate the influence of previous heroin use and non-MMT abstinence duration on IVFC. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging(rs-fMRI) data were acquired and analyzed to extract GM/WM-IVFC metrics, which were compared ROI-wise between groups and correlated with neuropsychological scales. Transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas(AHBA) were integrated via partial least squares(PLS) regression and functional enrichment analyses to further identify gene expression profiles underlying IVFC alterations. Results After Bonferroni correction, compared to HC1, MMT group exhibited the most widespread IVFC increases, spanning 20 GM and 7 WM regions. HSA group shared some overlapping GM-IVFC elevations with MMT group in bilateral orbital parts of inferior frontal gyrus and thalamus, yet its overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions was lower than that of MMT group. Neither OUD1 nor OUD2 showed difference in overall mean IVFC of significant GM regions from HC2. Both OUD1/2 displayed elevated overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions relative to HC2. Then, the overall mean IVFC of significant GM/WM regions between MMT group and HC1 were positively correlated with impulsivity, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and daily methadone dose. PLS regression linked IVFC patterns to AHBA transcriptomic profiles in MMT group, with enriched pathways in neuroinflammation, synaptic function, glutamatergic signaling, and neuronal development. Conclusions These findings indicate that MMT is accompanied by cerebral IVFC elevations, whose linkages with neuropsychological aberrations and gene profiles implicate IVFC as a latent clinical phenotype for managing MMT-related complications.

item.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

item.title: Association of scan time with resting-state functional connectivity discriminability: effects of temporal alignment.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is increasingly used to probe individual differences in brain organization, but individual-level FC discriminability may vary across repeated acquisitions related to arousal, physiology, and endogenous brain state. Acquisition-time variation may be a systematic contributor to this variability, yet its impact on FC discriminability has not been well characterized. Multi-session resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project were analyzed using minimally preprocessed and ICA-FIX-denoised BOLD time series. Whole-brain and network-level FC matrices were constructed after atlas-based parcellation, and sessions were grouped into one-hour daytime bins. Discriminability was computed to quantify how well repeated FC profiles from the same individual could be distinguished from those of other individuals, and grouped versus ungrouped estimates were compared. Temporal alignment of scans according to acquisition time substantially improved FC discriminability across both test-retest configurations. Whole-brain discriminability increased from 0.29 to 0.61 in one configuration and from 0.31 to 0.60 in the other. Similar gains were observed across canonical networks, with robust improvements in the default mode, dorsal attention, frontoparietal, and visual networks. These findings show that acquisition-time grouping was associated with higher FC discriminability in this HCP sample. Incorporating acquisition-time structure into rs-fMRI acquisition and analysis may enhance connectome fingerprinting and improve FC discriminability.

item.title: Complex Spatial and Temporal Organization of Functional Brain Networks
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent research exploring brain-behavior associations has relied on the language of complex systems to understand how stable behavioral individual differences emerge from brain function. At the same time, advances in neuroimaging have provided greater insight into both the topological and temporal properties of macroscale cortical networks. These new approaches offer a potential avenue for understanding how functional activity in the brain might behave in a manner that aligns with complex-systems interpretations of psychological traits. The present study used resting-state data from the Human Connectome project ( N = 994) to explore associations between the spatial and temporal features of functional brain networks. Using an adaptive frequency approach to explore brain function at different timescales together with a family of methods from complex systems theory, we identified patterns of brain state organization reflecting a state-trait continuum, with more stable trait-like dynamics and greater functional coupling between networks in lower frequency oscillations. Additionally, we found evidence of greater coupling across timescales in brain networks associated with higher-order cognition. This research supports interpretations of brain organization as a spatiotemporal hierarchy and provides future avenues for exploring brain-behavior associations from a complex system perspective.

item.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.
